units.excerpt: Our Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) is our voluntary framework for managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is described as a voluntary framework for managing catastrophic AI risk.

units.excerpt: It establishes how we identify and evaluate risks, how we make decisions about AI development and deployment, and, from the perspective of the world at large, how we aim to make sure that the benefits of our models exceed their costs.
units.paraphrase: The RSP covers risk identification, development/deployment decisions, and ensuring benefits exceed costs from a societal perspective.

units.excerpt: We have always intended for our RSP to be a living document.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is intended to be a living document.

units.excerpt: We will continually update the RSP as we learn more about AI capabilities and risks, develop and refine technical safety measures, and gain more experience navigating an ecosystem in which the risks to society depend on the actions of many developers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to continually updating the RSP as understanding of capabilities, risks, safety measures, and multi-developer dynamics improves.

units.excerpt: The major components of this third iteration are as follows:
units.paraphrase: This introduces a list of the major components of the third RSP iteration.

units.excerpt: Our recommendations for industry-wide safety outline what it would take, at an industry-wide level, to keep catastrophic risks reliably low through a period of rapid advances in AI capabilities.
units.paraphrase: The document introduces industry-wide safety recommendations aimed at keeping catastrophic risk low during rapid AI advances.

units.excerpt: We lay this out in a table that maps capability thresholds to the mitigations we believe they call for.
units.paraphrase: A table maps capability thresholds to corresponding mitigations.

units.excerpt: We also include our planned mitigations as a company, which are drawn from other sections of this policy and associated artifacts.
units.paraphrase: Company-specific planned mitigations, sourced from elsewhere in the policy, are also included.

units.excerpt: This approach represents a change from our previous RSP, driven by a collective action problem.
units.paraphrase: The new approach reflects a change from the prior RSP due to a collective action problem.

units.excerpt: The overall level of catastrophic risk from AI depends on the actions of multiple AI developers, not just one.
units.paraphrase: Catastrophic risk depends on the collective actions of multiple AI developers.

units.excerpt: Our previous RSP committed to implementing mitigations that would reduce our models' absolute risk levels to acceptable levels, without regard to whether other frontier AI developers would do the same.
units.paraphrase: The prior RSP focused on reducing absolute risk regardless of other developers' actions.

units.excerpt: But from a societal perspective, what matters is the risk to the ecosystem as a whole.
units.paraphrase: From a societal standpoint, ecosystem-wide risk is what matters.

units.excerpt: If one AI developer paused development to implement safety measures while others moved forward with training and deploying AI systems without strong mitigations, that could result in a world that is less safe—the developers with the weakest protections would set the pace, and responsible developers would lose their ability to do safety research and advance the public benefit.
units.paraphrase: Unilateral pausing by one developer while others proceed unsafely could make the world less safe overall.

units.excerpt: Although this situation has not yet arisen, it looks likely enough that we want to prepare for it.
units.paraphrase: This scenario has not occurred but seems likely enough to warrant preparation.

units.excerpt: We now separate our plans as a company—those which we expect to achieve regardless of what any other company does—from our more ambitious industry-wide recommendations.
units.paraphrase: Company-specific plans are now separated from broader industry-wide recommendations.

units.excerpt: We aspire to advance the latter through a mixture of example-setting, addressing unsolved technical problems, advocacy through industry groups, and policy advocacy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic aspires to advance industry-wide recommendations through example-setting, technical work, and advocacy.

units.excerpt: But we cannot commit to following them unilaterally.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic cannot unilaterally commit to the industry-wide recommendations.

units.excerpt: Frontier Safety Roadmaps are a new requirement under our RSP.
units.paraphrase: Frontier Safety Roadmaps are introduced as a new RSP requirement.

units.excerpt: These will describe our concrete plans for making progress across Security, Alignment, Safeguards, and Policy.
units.paraphrase: The Roadmaps will describe concrete plans across four domains: Security, Alignment, Safeguards, and Policy.

units.excerpt: Goals described in the Roadmaps are intended to be ambitious, yet achievable—providing the kind of forcing function that we consider to be a past success of our RSP.
units.paraphrase: Roadmap goals are meant to be ambitious yet achievable, functioning as a forcing mechanism that has worked well previously.

units.excerpt: These are not hard commitments but rather public goals against which we will openly grade our progress.
units.paraphrase: Roadmap goals are not binding commitments but public benchmarks for self-assessment.

units.excerpt: Risk Reports are another new requirement. Risk Reports will provide detailed information on the safety profile of our models at the time of publication.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports are introduced as a new requirement providing detailed safety-profile information at publication time.

units.excerpt: They will go beyond describing model capabilities, addressing our thinking on how capabilities, threat models (the specific ways that models might pose threats), and active risk mitigations fit together, providing an assessment of the overall level of risk.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports will integrate capabilities, threat models, and mitigations into an overall risk assessment.

units.excerpt: These reports will reflect our reasoning as to whether we believe the risks of training or deploying our models are justified by their corresponding benefits to the world.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports will explain whether the risks of training/deploying models are justified by their benefits.

units.excerpt: They will be published online, with some redactions to protect sensitive details about, for example, our training methods and organizations with whom we work.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports will be published online with redactions of sensitive information.

units.excerpt: As detailed below, we also aim to subject Risk Reports to review by credible, independent external parties.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports are also intended to undergo review by credible independent external parties.

units.excerpt: Finally, our governance commitments are intended to promote internal and external accountability, similar to those in our previous RSP.
units.paraphrase: Governance commitments aim to promote accountability, consistent with the prior RSP.

units.excerpt: Our RSP is only one part of our overall approach to safety.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is only one component of the broader safety approach.

units.excerpt: For instance, although this policy focuses on catastrophic risks, they are not the only risks we consider important—our Usage Policy and societal impacts research address other concerns.
units.paraphrase: Other risks beyond catastrophic risk are addressed by the Usage Policy and societal impacts research.

units.excerpt: Further, the RSP may serve some regulatory requirements, but it is not designed to be comprehensive.
units.paraphrase: The RSP may partially fulfill regulatory requirements but is not intended as a comprehensive compliance document.

units.excerpt: We want to keep it focused on our most central measures for addressing the catastrophic risks we prioritize most, rather than expand it to address every obligation we face.
units.paraphrase: The RSP is deliberately kept focused on core catastrophic-risk measures rather than every obligation.

units.excerpt: Where regulatory requirements exceed or differ from what the RSP covers, we will address them through separate documents.
units.paraphrase: Additional or differing regulatory requirements will be addressed in separate documents.

units.excerpt: "Catastrophic risk" as used in our RSP refers generally to risks of the most severe potential harms from advanced AI, such as existential threats or fundamental destabilization of global systems.
units.paraphrase: Catastrophic risk is defined broadly as the most severe potential harms, including existential threats or global destabilization.

units.excerpt: We use this term in its plain meaning rather than adopting any specific statutory definition.
units.paraphrase: The term is used in its plain meaning, not tied to a specific statutory definition.

units.excerpt: Where laws such as California SB 53 define this or similar terms with specific thresholds, we address those requirements in separate compliance frameworks.
units.paraphrase: Legal definitions such as those in California SB 53 are addressed via separate compliance frameworks.

units.excerpt: This section outlines our recommendations for what it would take, at an industry-wide level, to keep catastrophic risks reliably low through a period of rapid advances in AI capabilities.
units.paraphrase: This section presents recommendations for industry-wide safety during rapid AI capability growth.

units.excerpt: We lay this out in a three-column table.
units.paraphrase: The recommendations are presented in a three-column table.

units.excerpt: The left column identifies capability thresholds that would call for heightened mitigations.
units.paraphrase: The left column of the table lists capability thresholds triggering heightened mitigations.

units.excerpt: The middle column provides an overview of our planned mitigations, which we have set forth more fully in our Frontier Safety Roadmap and other sections of this policy.
units.paraphrase: The middle column summarizes company mitigations detailed elsewhere in the policy and Roadmap.

units.excerpt: The right column describes our recommendations for industry-wide safety at each threshold.
units.paraphrase: The right column contains industry-wide safety recommendations for each threshold.

units.excerpt: The distinction between our plans as a company (middle column) and our industry-wide recommendations (right column) reflects the limitations of any single AI developer's ability to ensure safety across the industry.
units.paraphrase: The company/industry-wide distinction reflects limits on a single developer's ability to ensure industry-wide safety.

units.excerpt: In particular, we cannot unilaterally and unconditionally commit to staying in line with the industry-wide recommendations in the right column.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic cannot unconditionally commit unilaterally to the right-column recommendations.

units.excerpt: However, these recommendations will drive important aspects of our work:
units.paraphrase: The recommendations will nonetheless shape important aspects of Anthropic's work.

units.context_stem: However, these recommendations will drive important aspects of our work:
units.excerpt: We use these recommendations as the north star for our risk mitigations planning as well as our public policy work.
units.paraphrase: The recommendations serve as the guiding standard for risk mitigation planning and public policy work.

units.context_stem: However, these recommendations will drive important aspects of our work:
units.excerpt: We will strive to advance these recommendations through a mixture of example-setting, addressing unsolved technical problems, advocacy through industry groups, and policy advocacy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will try to advance these recommendations through example-setting, technical work, and advocacy.

units.context_stem: However, these recommendations will drive important aspects of our work:
units.excerpt: We have also adopted a set of competitor-contingent commitments (see Appendix A) aimed at staying in line with these recommendations in scenarios where we can be confident that other relevant AI developers are doing the same.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic has adopted commitments contingent on competitors' behavior, detailed in Appendix A.

units.excerpt: At this point in AI's rapid development, we cannot presently give highly specific advance detail on what evaluations will determine whether risk thresholds have been passed, or what risk mitigations will be needed to achieve safety.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic cannot currently specify detailed evaluations for risk thresholds or the mitigations safety would require.

units.excerpt: Our recommendations for industry-wide safety are thus structured around requiring analysis and arguments making a strong case for safety, rather than AI Safety Levels (more in Appendix B).
units.paraphrase: Recommendations are built around requiring safety-case arguments rather than fixed AI Safety Levels.

units.excerpt: This leaves flexibility in how risk thresholds are evaluated and how safety is achieved and argued for.
units.paraphrase: The safety-case approach allows flexibility in evaluating thresholds and achieving/arguing safety.

units.excerpt: But it creates a challenge: one actor's view of what constitutes good risk assessment and mitigation may be very different from another's.
units.paraphrase: This flexibility creates a challenge since different actors may hold very different standards for adequate risk assessment.

units.excerpt: Ultimately, the best way for these recommendations to be implemented is likely via governance of all relevant frontier AI developers by third parties that determine which developers need to provide risk analyses and make arguments for the safety of their systems, and determine which such arguments are adequate.
units.paraphrase: Implementation is best achieved through third-party governance determining which developers must provide risk analyses and assessing their adequacy.

units.excerpt: To the extent this takes the form of national regulation, different countries should attempt to harmonize their governance, including standards of evidence, to avoid a race to the bottom.
units.paraphrase: National regulations should be harmonized across countries to prevent a race to the bottom.

units.excerpt: In the shorter run, independent bodies (standards-setting organizations, auditors, etc.) might review such arguments and enforce high quality standards for private AI developers via voluntary mechanisms.
units.paraphrase: In the near term, independent bodies could review safety arguments and enforce quality standards voluntarily.

units.excerpt: We expect that the recommendations for industry-wide safety will evolve significantly, as we learn more about AI capabilities, threat models, and risk mitigations.
units.paraphrase: The industry-wide recommendations are expected to evolve significantly as understanding improves.

units.excerpt: We hope these recommendations will become increasingly specific over time.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the recommendations will grow more specific over time.

units.excerpt: Note that an AI developer might provide a single analysis covering a broad category of models, such that there isn't a new analysis needed for each release.
units.paraphrase: A single analysis could cover a broad category of models rather than requiring one per release.

units.excerpt: Additionally, determinations of which AI developers need to provide such analysis should be made with an effort to spare smaller AI developers from unnecessary compliance burden.
units.paraphrase: Determinations of which developers must provide analysis should try to spare smaller developers unnecessary compliance burden.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: AI systems with the ability to significantly help individuals or groups with basic technical backgrounds (e.g., undergraduate STEM degrees) create/obtain and deploy chemical and/or biological weapons with serious potential for catastrophic damages.
units.paraphrase: The threshold covers AI systems that could significantly help lower-skilled individuals or groups create and deploy chemical/biological weapons with serious catastrophic potential.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: We will maintain or improve on our ASL-3 protections, which include classifier guards at least as robust as our initial Constitutional Classifiers; access controls for trusted users with exemptions to classifier guards; red-teaming, bug bounties, and threat intelligence for continually assessing the threat of jailbreaks; and a number of noteworthy security controls.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain or improve ASL-3 protections including classifier guards, access controls, and ongoing red-teaming/threat intelligence.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: Specifics may change, but we will maintain equally or more robust measures over time and will publish updates in our Risk Reports.
units.paraphrase: Specific measures may change but robustness will be maintained or improved, with updates published in Risk Reports.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: We expect to continuously meet the criteria in the right column, although we cannot make guarantees about an evolving landscape with continually adaptive attackers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects to continuously meet the industry-wide criteria but cannot guarantee this given adaptive attackers.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: A frontier developer should make a strong argument that individual users and relatively small teams will not become significantly more likely to cause catastrophic harm via their usage of product surfaces or via theft of model weights.
units.paraphrase: Industry-wide recommendation: developers should argue that small teams/individual users won't gain significantly increased ability to cause catastrophic harm via product use or weight theft.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations / bullet 1
units.excerpt: Restrictions on model behavior, and/or measures for quickly detecting and acting on Usage Policy violations, accompanied by a strong case that these measures are difficult to reliably, sustainably circumvent via jailbreaking.
units.paraphrase: Recommended measures include behavior restrictions and rapid detection/enforcement against Usage Policy violations, backed by a robust anti-jailbreak case.

units.locator: Table 1 / Non-novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations / bullet 2
units.excerpt: Precautions against opportunistic theft of model weights, such as centralized controls on third-party applications and software updates.
units.paraphrase: Recommended measures include precautions against opportunistic weight theft, such as centralized third-party app and update controls.

units.excerpt: This column summarizes commitments drawn from other sections of this policy and associated artifacts. It should be read as an overview, not as indicating any separate or additional plans.
units.paraphrase: The middle column is a summary of commitments described elsewhere, not a source of new obligations.

units.locator: Table 1 / Novel chemical/biological weapons production / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: AI systems with the ability to significantly help threat actors (for example, moderately resourced expert-backed teams) create/obtain and deploy chemical and/or biological weapons with potential for catastrophic damages far beyond those of past catastrophes such as COVID-19.
units.paraphrase: The threshold covers AI systems that could significantly help moderately resourced expert-backed threat actors create weapons causing damage far beyond COVID-19.

units.locator: Table 1 / Novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: Novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: We will apply protections at least as strong as our ASL-3 protections (see previous row) to an expanded set of potential use cases for AI, covering the most likely vectors for this threat.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3-level protections will be extended to cover more use cases relevant to this expanded threat.

units.locator: Table 1 / Novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: Novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: Additionally, we will identify the most concerning specific threat pathways, create policy recommendations for early detection and response for such threats, and share this content with policymakers.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will identify concerning threat pathways, create early-detection policy recommendations, and share them with policymakers.

units.locator: Table 1 / Novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: A frontier developer should make a strong argument that threat actors will not become significantly more likely to cause the sort of catastrophic harm discussed in the lefthand column via their usage of product surfaces or via theft of model weights.
units.paraphrase: Developers should argue that threat actors won't gain significantly greater catastrophic capability via product use or weight theft.

units.locator: Table 1 / Novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This will likely require similar measures to those from the previous row, but to a higher standard—to the point where even well-resourced and -staffed threat actors would be unlikely to reliably jailbreak models or cause catastrophic harm via unauthorized access to or modification of models (including via stolen or modified model weights).
units.paraphrase: A higher standard than the prior row is needed, sufficient to resist even well-resourced threat actors from jailbreaking or causing harm via unauthorized access.

units.locator: Table 1 / Novel chemical/biological weapons production / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Novel chemical/biological weapons production; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This would likely mean security roughly in line with RAND SL4, but it depends on the capabilities of the strongest and most plausible threat actors that are not bound by a credible governance regime enforcing the recommendations for industry-wide safety outlined here.
units.paraphrase: This implies security around RAND SL4, contingent on the capability of the strongest unbound threat actors.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: AI systems that are highly relied on and have extensive access to sensitive assets as well as moderate capacity for autonomous, goal-directed operation and subterfuge—such that it is plausible these AI systems could (if directed toward this goal, either deliberately or inadvertently) carry out sabotage leading to irreversibly and substantially higher odds of a later global catastrophe.
units.paraphrase: The threshold covers highly relied-upon AI systems with sensitive access and moderate autonomous/goal-directed capacity that could plausibly cause sabotage raising odds of later global catastrophe.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: In the near term, this possibility will likely be most applicable to AI systems that are extensively used within major AI companies, with the opportunity to manipulate how their successor systems are trained and deployed as well as the evidence used to assess their safety.
units.paraphrase: Near-term, this applies mainly to AI systems used internally at major AI companies that could manipulate training or safety evidence of successor systems.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: Down the line, this possibility may come to apply to AI systems deployed within government and other high-stakes settings.
units.paraphrase: In the future, this threshold may extend to AI systems used in government and other high-stakes settings.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: We will detail the state of our AI systems' capabilities and propensities, our monitoring practices, and the overall level of risk in our Risk Reports.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports will detail AI capabilities/propensities, monitoring practices, and overall risk level for this threshold.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: We expect to continually be able to meet the criteria in the right column, although we cannot make guarantees about an evolving technology that may increasingly have the ability to detect and manipulate testing.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects to meet the right-column criteria but cannot guarantee this given evolving technology capable of detecting/manipulating testing.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: A frontier developer should make a strong argument that AI systems will not carry out sabotage leading to irreversibly and substantially higher odds of a later global catastrophe.
units.paraphrase: Developers should argue AI systems will not cause sabotage that substantially raises odds of later global catastrophe.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This case may initially be relatively simple and rely heavily on capability limitations, if it is first required when the risk is merely plausible.
units.paraphrase: The safety case may initially rely on capability limitations if required only when risk is merely plausible.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: High-stakes sabotage opportunities; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: As risk becomes harder to rule out, this case will likely include some combination of:
units.paraphrase: As risk becomes harder to exclude, the safety case will likely combine several measures.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations / bullet 1
units.context_stem: As risk becomes harder to rule out, this case will likely include some combination of:
units.excerpt: Internal compartmentalization, restriction, and code review to prevent excessive sabotage opportunities for AI models.
units.paraphrase: Measure: internal compartmentalization, restriction, and code review to limit sabotage opportunities.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations / bullet 2
units.context_stem: As risk becomes harder to rule out, this case will likely include some combination of:
units.excerpt: Capability assessments demonstrating that AI models lack the ability to carry out irreversible (which would generally mean unnoticed) sabotage.
units.paraphrase: Measure: capability assessments showing models lack ability for irreversible/unnoticed sabotage.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations / bullet 3
units.context_stem: As risk becomes harder to rule out, this case will likely include some combination of:
units.excerpt: Monitoring and/or restricting AI behavior and usage internally.
units.paraphrase: Measure: internal monitoring and/or restriction of AI behavior and usage.

units.locator: Table 1 / High-stakes sabotage opportunities / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations / bullet 4
units.context_stem: As risk becomes harder to rule out, this case will likely include some combination of:
units.excerpt: Evidence that AI models lack the propensity to deceive, manipulate, or sabotage users.
units.paraphrase: Measure: evidence demonstrating models lack the propensity to deceive, manipulate, or sabotage users.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: AI systems that can fully automate, or otherwise dramatically accelerate, the work of large, top-tier teams of human researchers in domains where fast progress could cause threats to international security and/or rapid disruptions to the global balance of power—for example, energy, robotics, weapons development and AI itself.
units.paraphrase: The threshold covers AI able to fully automate or dramatically accelerate top-tier research teams in domains where fast progress threatens international security or the global balance of power.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: For now, our evaluations will focus specifically on AI R&D, as this domain likely plays to AI systems' current strengths and is more tractable to assess than capabilities in other domains.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations currently focus on AI R&D since it fits AI systems' current strengths and is easier to assess.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: Additionally, AI R&D alone could cause acceleration in AI capabilities improvements, to the point where all of the threats listed above (and more) develop very quickly.
units.paraphrase: AI R&D acceleration alone could speed up development of all other listed threats.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: We will consider this threshold to be met if we determine that either (1) our models would be able to fully substitute for our entire set of Research Scientists and Research Engineers, at competitive costs (i.e., within a factor of 5); or (2) there is "dramatic acceleration" of the pace of AI progress for reasons that likely relate to the automation of AI R&D.
units.paraphrase: The threshold is met if models can fully substitute for the entire Research Scientist/Engineer workforce within 5x cost, or if AI R&D automation causes dramatic acceleration of AI progress.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: We would consider scenario (2) to have occurred where (a) we observe or expect double the rate of progress in AI aggregate capabilities compared to the rate we'd expect in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D and (b) it is plausible that this doubling is substantially attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering (as opposed to other factors, such as increased headcount, compute, or general productivity), such that continuation of the trend in AI progress could lead to even greater acceleration.
units.paraphrase: Scenario 2 is defined as observing/expecting a doubling of AI progress rate plausibly due to automation of research/engineering rather than other factors, potentially leading to further acceleration.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: This capability threshold is intended to reflect our definition of highly capable models (see Section 3.6).
units.paraphrase: This threshold reflects the framework's definition of highly capable models.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Capability or usage threshold
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Capability or usage threshold
units.excerpt: It may be sensible to add earlier, and/or easier-to-measure, thresholds that trigger less demanding versions of the mitigations for this threshold.
units.paraphrase: Additional earlier or more measurable thresholds triggering lighter mitigations might be added.

units.excerpt: "Double the rate of progress" means "as much progress in one year as one would see in two years at baseline."
units.paraphrase: Double the rate of progress is defined as achieving in one year what would normally take two years.

units.excerpt: For example, if baseline progress involved a 3x scaleup in compute and a 3x improvement in algorithmic efficiency (for a 9x "effective scaleup"), "double the rate of progress" would entail something like an 81x effective scaleup.
units.paraphrase: Example: baseline 9x effective scaleup would correspond to about 81x effective scaleup under double-rate progress.

units.excerpt: This is not the same idea as "doubling researchers' productivity," since doubling inputs does not necessarily double the rate of progress.
units.paraphrase: Doubling the rate of progress differs from doubling researcher productivity, since input doubling doesn't necessarily double progress rate.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—our plan as a company / bullet 1
units.excerpt: Resource and complete significant "moonshot R&D for security" projects, to explore ambitious and possibly unconventional ways to achieve unprecedented levels of security against the world's best-resourced attackers.
units.paraphrase: Commitment to fund and complete ambitious moonshot security R&D projects targeting unprecedented security levels.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—our plan as a company / bullet 2
units.excerpt: Achieve an "eyes on everything" state for our internal AI development. We will comprehensively gather, centralize, and maintain logs for all critical AI-development activities, and use AI to analyze them for issues including security threats, concerning behavior by insiders (humans as well as AI systems themselves), and training processes or data that are out of line with the public Constitution that shapes and defines our AI models.
units.paraphrase: Commitment to achieve comprehensive internal monitoring ('eyes on everything'), logging all critical development activities and using AI to analyze for security threats, insider issues, and Constitution deviations.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—our plan as a company / bullet 3
units.excerpt: Perform systematic alignment assessments to examine Claude's behavioral patterns and propensities, meaningfully incorporating mechanistic interpretability and adversarial red-teaming to test our auditing methods.
units.paraphrase: Commitment to systematic alignment assessments of Claude's behavior using interpretability and adversarial red-teaming.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—our plan as a company / bullet 4
units.excerpt: Develop our internal red-teaming of our deployment safeguards to the point where our internal red-teaming performs better at finding potential jailbreaks than the collective abilities of the participants in our established bug bounty programs.
units.paraphrase: Commitment to develop internal red-teaming that outperforms the collective bug-bounty participant pool at finding jailbreaks.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—our plan as a company / bullet 5
units.excerpt: Publish Risk Reports with the status of, and noteworthy findings from, all of the above, subject to external review by at least one expert, experienced, credible, candid and disinterested external party.
units.paraphrase: Commitment to publish Risk Reports on the above efforts, subject to review by at least one qualified independent external party.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—our plan as a company
units.excerpt: We broadly expect to lead the industry in practices that reduce the risks from AI, although we cannot unilaterally make guarantees about the safety level of AI this advanced.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects to lead the industry on risk-reducing practices but cannot guarantee safety at this advanced capability level unilaterally.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: A frontier developer should make a strong argument that: No user or team of users (including those backed by top-tier states) will become significantly more likely to cause catastrophic harm via their usage of product surfaces or via theft of model weights.
units.paraphrase: Developers should argue that no user or team, including state-backed ones, gains significantly greater catastrophic capability via product use or weight theft.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This will likely require similar measures to those listed in row 1, but to a higher standard‚ to the point where even well-resourced and -staffed threat actors would be unlikely to reliably jailbreak models or cause catastrophic harm via unauthorized access to or modification of models (including via stolen or modified model weights).
units.paraphrase: Similar measures to row 1 are needed but at a higher standard sufficient to resist well-resourced threat actors.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: Accomplishing this would likely mean security roughly in line with RAND SL4. Security requirements would be calibrated to defend against the strongest plausible threat actors who are not bound by a credible industry-wide safety regime.
units.paraphrase: This implies RAND SL4-level security, calibrated to the strongest unbound plausible threat actors.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: Actors subject to such a regime would not need to be treated as threats to each other's model weights.
units.paraphrase: Developers covered by a credible governance regime need not treat each other as weight-theft threats.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: Even malicious employees and other insiders with maximal levels of access will not be significantly enabled to cause catastrophic harm.
units.paraphrase: Even maximally-privileged malicious insiders should not gain significant ability to cause catastrophic harm.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This requires (among other things) accounting for internal tools that are less restricted than product surfaces, and for the possibility of unauthorized modification of models.
units.paraphrase: This requires accounting for less-restricted internal tools and possible unauthorized model modification.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This will likely require an internal Usage Policy and strong internal compartmentalization, controls and/or monitoring to restrict the ability of employees and contractors (up to and including the company's CEO as well as its most privileged technical employees) to circumvent the Usage Policy.
units.paraphrase: An internal Usage Policy with strong compartmentalization and controls is needed to prevent even the CEO or top technical employees from circumventing it.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: AI models have not been deliberately or inadvertently trained with dangerous goals, or are otherwise unlikely to autonomously cause catastrophic harm.
units.paraphrase: Models must not have been trained with dangerous goals, deliberately or inadvertently, and are otherwise unlikely to autonomously cause catastrophic harm.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: This will likely require similar measures to those listed above under "High-stakes sabotage opportunities" (some combination of internal compartmentalization, restriction and code review; monitoring AI behavior; and evidence that AI models lack the propensity to deceive and manipulate users), but to a greater degree.
units.paraphrase: Similar measures to the sabotage row apply here but to a greater degree.

units.locator: Table 1 / Automated R&D in key domains / Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.context_stem: Row: Automated R&D in key domains; Column: Mitigations—ambitious industry-wide recommendations
units.excerpt: In particular, at this point AI systems might be responsible for much of the research and analysis that underpins risk assessment, and might have strong capabilities for deception, manipulation and obfuscation of evidence, in which case analyses of threats from AIs should follow very high evidentiary standards with thorough and careful analysis of the possibility that much of the key evidence is suspect due to the possibility of manipulation by AI systems.
units.paraphrase: Because AI may underpin risk-assessment research and could have strong deceptive capabilities, threat analyses should apply very high evidentiary standards accounting for possible evidence manipulation.

units.excerpt: We will maintain a Frontier Safety Roadmap laying out ambitious but achievable goals for improving our risk mitigations—charting our progress as a company and raising the bar over time.
units.paraphrase: The Frontier Safety Roadmap will set ambitious, achievable risk-mitigation goals and track progress over time.

units.excerpt: Maintaining and reporting on this Roadmap is part of our work under the RSP.
units.paraphrase: Maintaining and reporting the Roadmap is part of RSP obligations.

units.excerpt: It will be shared with all full-time employees as well as our Board of Directors (Board) and Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), and published in redacted form.
units.paraphrase: The Roadmap will be shared internally with employees, the Board, and the LTBT, and published externally in redacted form.

units.excerpt: We will provide updates on whether we achieve the goals, and set new goals when we do.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will report on goal achievement and set new goals as prior ones are met.

units.excerpt: Our Frontier Safety Roadmap is subject to change.
units.paraphrase: The Roadmap may change over time.

units.excerpt: Some changes may simply reflect our evolving understanding of how best to mitigate key risks.
units.paraphrase: Changes to the Roadmap may reflect evolving understanding of risk mitigation.

units.excerpt: However, we will strive to avoid situations where we revise the goals in a less ambitious direction simply because we are unable to achieve them.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will try to avoid weakening goals merely because they proved hard to achieve.

units.excerpt: By establishing this expectation, we hope to create a forcing function for work that would otherwise be challenging to appropriately prioritize and resource, as it requires collaboration (and in some cases sacrifices) from multiple parts of the company and can be at cross-purposes with immediate competitive and commercial priorities.
units.paraphrase: This expectation is meant to force prioritization of cross-company collaborative work that competes with commercial priorities.

units.excerpt: Publishing our Frontier Safety Roadmap may also help inform broader industry and policy discussions on AI safety.
units.paraphrase: Publishing the Roadmap could contribute to wider industry and policy discussions on AI safety.

units.excerpt: Our current Frontier Safety Roadmap is available at anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap.
units.paraphrase: The current Roadmap is published at a specified URL.

units.excerpt: We will also keep past Roadmaps available at that link.
units.paraphrase: Past Roadmap versions will remain available at the same link.

units.excerpt: We will publish Risk Reports discussing the risks of our systems and how we have made determinations about whether to continue AI development and deployment in light of the risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will publish Risk Reports that discuss system risks and the determinations made about continuing AI development and deployment.

units.excerpt: These have significant content in common with system cards, but we are adding additional structure and process aimed at presenting our overall assessments of risk.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports overlap with system cards but include added structure and process for presenting overall risk assessments.

units.excerpt: A Risk Report will cover all publicly deployed models at the time of its publication.
units.paraphrase: Each Risk Report will cover all models publicly deployed as of its publication date.

units.excerpt: It will also cover internally deployed models when we determine that these models could pose significant risks beyond those posed by models that are covered by a prior Risk Report.
units.paraphrase: Internally deployed models will also be covered if they are judged to pose significant risks not already addressed in a prior Risk Report.

units.excerpt: While there are a variety of reasons we might classify an internal model this way, this will—at a minimum—include any internal models that we are deploying for large-scale, fully autonomous research.
units.paraphrase: At minimum, internal models used for large-scale fully autonomous research will be classified as posing significant risk.

units.excerpt: Models fitting the above description are abbreviated below as "in-scope models."
units.paraphrase: Models meeting the described criteria are termed "in-scope models" in the document.

units.excerpt: We may also voluntarily include additional models in a Risk Report, e.g., to contribute to general discourse, but such inclusion does not expand the commitments below.
units.paraphrase: Additional models may be voluntarily included in a Risk Report without expanding the stated commitments.

units.excerpt: We will publish a Risk Report every 3-6 months.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports will be published on a 3-6 month cadence.

units.excerpt: Note that unlike system cards, Risk Reports will not be published with each new model release.
units.paraphrase: Unlike system cards, Risk Reports are not tied to each new model release.

units.excerpt: When we publicly deploy a model that we determine is significantly more capable than any of the models covered in the most recent Risk Report, we will publish a discussion (in our System Card or elsewhere) of how that model's capabilities and propensities affect or change analysis in the Risk Report.
units.paraphrase: If a newly publicly deployed model is significantly more capable than any model in the latest Risk Report, a discussion of its impact on the analysis will be published.

units.excerpt: Within 30 days of determining that we have an internally deployed model that is in-scope (per the description above), we will publish a discussion (in a System Card or elsewhere) of how that model's capabilities and propensities affect or change the analysis in the Risk Report.
units.paraphrase: Within 30 days of identifying an in-scope internally deployed model, a discussion of its effect on the Risk Report analysis will be published.

units.excerpt: Specifically, risks arising from the capability thresholds in our recommendations for industry-wide safety (see Section 1).
units.paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that significant risks refer to those arising from capability thresholds in the industry-wide safety recommendations.

units.excerpt: Several principles guide how we approach Risk Reports:
units.paraphrase: The section introduces guiding principles for Risk Reports.

units.context_stem: Several principles guide how we approach Risk Reports:
units.excerpt: We intend for our Risk Reports to be direct, candid, and informative about how we see the risks of our systems and our state of preparedness for them.
units.paraphrase: Risk Reports are intended to be direct, candid, and informative regarding risk perception and preparedness.

units.context_stem: Several principles guide how we approach Risk Reports:
units.excerpt: In particular, we will acknowledge when we view certain models as posing significant risks in absolute terms, even if our marginal contribution to overall ecosystem risk may be relatively limited when taking other developers' AI models into account.
units.paraphrase: Significant absolute risks of certain models will be acknowledged even when Anthropic's marginal contribution to ecosystem risk is limited.

units.context_stem: Several principles guide how we approach Risk Reports:
units.excerpt: We will put significant effort into investigating (for example, via capability evaluations) the case for risk, and into sharing what we find.
units.paraphrase: Significant effort will be invested in investigating the case for risk and sharing findings.

units.context_stem: Several principles guide how we approach Risk Reports:
units.excerpt: When a Risk Report describes risk mitigations we have in place (or plan to implement shortly), we will keep our future practices in line with this description or track and report noteworthy changes and deviations (generally via subsequent Risk Reports).
units.paraphrase: Future practices will either match described mitigations or noteworthy deviations will be tracked and reported in later Risk Reports.

units.context_stem: When a Risk Report describes risk mitigations we have in place...
units.excerpt: We should make a strong attempt to ensure that ongoing (as opposed to temporary) changes do not significantly increase the level of risk.
units.paraphrase: A strong effort should be made to ensure ongoing changes do not meaningfully raise risk levels.

units.excerpt: We will describe how we identify, evaluate, and mitigate catastrophic risks.
units.paraphrase: The report will describe the process of identifying, evaluating, and mitigating catastrophic risks.

units.excerpt: A Risk Report will document the following:
units.paraphrase: The following items will be documented in a Risk Report.

units.context_stem: Factual information. A Risk Report will document the following:
units.excerpt: Threat model identification: Our criteria for determining which catastrophic risks (i.e., threat models) we assess.
units.paraphrase: The report will state the criteria used to determine which catastrophic risk threat models are assessed.

units.context_stem: Factual information. A Risk Report will document the following:
units.excerpt: Threat model specification: The relevant threat models (which will, at a minimum, include those discussed above).
units.paraphrase: The report will specify relevant threat models, including at least those already discussed.

units.context_stem: Factual information. A Risk Report will document the following:
units.excerpt: Evidence (including evaluations) about relevant model capabilities and behaviors: For each in-scope model, capability and alignment evaluations (conducted internally and by external parties as appropriate), their results, and (as appropriate) other evidence we considered in assessing the level of risk.
units.paraphrase: For each in-scope model, the report will present capability/alignment evaluations, results, and other relevant risk evidence.

units.context_stem: Factual information. A Risk Report will document the following:
units.excerpt: Risk mitigations: For each in-scope model, the mitigations we are implementing across security, deployment safeguards, and alignment domains, along with discussion of their effectiveness.
units.paraphrase: For each in-scope model, the mitigations across security, deployment, and alignment domains and their effectiveness will be documented.

units.context_stem: Factual information. A Risk Report will document the following:
units.excerpt: Additional relevant factors: Any other considerations material to our risk analysis.
units.paraphrase: Other considerations material to the risk analysis will also be documented.

units.excerpt: Risk analyses. We will provide our reasoning and conclusions regarding both specific threat models and overall risk levels.
units.paraphrase: The report will provide reasoning and conclusions about both specific threat models and overall risk levels.

units.excerpt: Threat-specific risk assessment: For each threat model, we will analyze remaining absolute risk–i.e., the leftover risk after accounting for our mitigations.
units.paraphrase: For each threat model, the remaining absolute risk after mitigations will be analyzed.

units.excerpt: We will also discuss whether we believe we've crossed relevant thresholds in our recommendations for industry-wide safety (see Section 1), and (as relevant) whether we believe we're meeting the risk mitigation standards corresponding to them.
units.paraphrase: The report will discuss whether relevant industry-wide safety thresholds have been crossed and whether corresponding mitigation standards are being met.

units.excerpt: Overall risk assessment: We will provide an overall risk assessment.
units.paraphrase: An overall risk assessment will be provided.

units.excerpt: Risk-benefit determination: We will explain whether, and if so why, we believe the identified risks are justified by corresponding benefits.
units.paraphrase: The report will explain whether identified risks are justified by corresponding benefits.

units.excerpt: Looking forward: We will outline our plans for continuing to monitor and mitigate the relevant risks over time.
units.paraphrase: Plans to continue monitoring and mitigating risks over time will be outlined.

units.excerpt: Review of past Risk Reports and decisions. We will address:
units.paraphrase: The report will include a review of past Risk Reports and decisions.

units.context_stem: Review of past Risk Reports and decisions. We will address:
units.excerpt: Changes in risk mitigation practices—noteworthy cases in which our risk mitigation practices deviated (including temporarily) or changed from what we discussed in our previous Risk Report over the relevant period, and their implications for the overall level of risk.
units.paraphrase: Noteworthy deviations or changes in risk mitigation practices since the prior Risk Report, and their risk implications, will be addressed.

units.context_stem: Review of past Risk Reports and decisions. We will address:
units.excerpt: Decisions to internally deploy in-scope models that would not otherwise be reviewed in a Risk Report (because they happened in between Risk Reports).
units.paraphrase: The report will cover decisions to internally deploy in-scope models that occurred between Risk Reports and were not otherwise reviewed.

units.context_stem: Decisions to internally deploy in-scope models...
units.excerpt: We will discuss how these decisions were made and whether they appear reasonable in light of any noteworthy new information that has come to light since then.
units.paraphrase: The report will discuss how such deployment decisions were made and their reasonableness given new information.

units.context_stem: Review of past Risk Reports and decisions. We will address:
units.excerpt: Changes to our Frontier Safety Roadmap and any cases where we failed to meet our goals.
units.paraphrase: Changes to the Frontier Safety Roadmap and any missed goals will be addressed.

units.excerpt: Marginal risk and ecosystem analysis. If we determine that the absolute level of risk being imposed industry-wide by AI systems such as ours is high, and are justifying our decision to move forward based partly on a marginal risk analysis, we will additionally address the following:
units.paraphrase: If industry-wide risk is judged high and marginal risk analysis partly justifies proceeding, additional topics will be addressed.

units.context_stem: we will additionally address the following:
units.excerpt: Competitive landscape analysis: What we know about how our current and future model capabilities and risk mitigations compare to those of relevant competitors.
units.paraphrase: The report will describe how model capabilities and mitigations compare to competitors.

units.context_stem: we will additionally address the following:
units.excerpt: Role in risk assessment: How these comparisons factored into our risk assessment.
units.paraphrase: How competitor comparisons influenced the risk assessment will be described.

units.context_stem: we will additionally address the following:
units.excerpt: Benefits analysis: The benefits, if any, of continuing to maintain our existing models or of advancing frontier capabilities, including considerations related to our mission and our ability to contribute to AI safety research and policy development.
units.paraphrase: Any benefits of maintaining existing models or advancing frontier capabilities, including mission-related considerations, will be analyzed.

units.context_stem: we will additionally address the following:
units.excerpt: Advocacy efforts: The steps we took to raise public awareness of the relevant risks and to encourage appropriate regulatory action, including our engagement with policymakers and other AI developers.
units.paraphrase: Advocacy steps taken to raise awareness and encourage regulation, including policymaker and industry engagement, will be described.

units.excerpt: We will conduct the assessments above with respect to each in-scope model.
units.paraphrase: The described assessments will be conducted for each in-scope model.

units.excerpt: To avoid redundancy, we will likely analyze similar models collectively rather than individually, with appropriate justification for any such groupings.
units.paraphrase: Similar models may be analyzed together rather than individually, with justification, to reduce redundancy.

units.excerpt: Initial assessment and drafting: Our internal subject matter experts will conduct risk assessments and draft the Risk Report.
units.paraphrase: Internal subject matter experts will conduct risk assessments and draft the Risk Report.

units.excerpt: Review and feedback: We will solicit comprehensive internal feedback on the report, focusing on identifying potential methodological weaknesses, analytical gaps, or areas requiring additional evidence or clarification.
units.paraphrase: Comprehensive internal feedback will be sought to identify methodological weaknesses, gaps, or needed clarifications.

units.excerpt: We may also use this feedback to improve or refine the report itself.
units.paraphrase: Feedback may be used to refine the report.

units.excerpt: We will usually also seek feedback from trusted external parties with relevant expertise.
units.paraphrase: Feedback from trusted external experts will usually also be sought.

units.excerpt: Executive approval: The Risk Report, along with the internal feedback and any available external feedback, will be sent to the CEO and Responsible Scaling Officer (RSO) for final review and approval.
units.paraphrase: The Risk Report and feedback will be sent to the CEO and RSO for final review and approval.

units.excerpt: The CEO and RSO will make the ultimate determination regarding the adequacy of the risk assessment and any downstream deployment or development plans.
units.paraphrase: The CEO and RSO make the final determination on the adequacy of the risk assessment and related deployment or development plans.

units.excerpt: Governance notification: Following approval of a Risk Report, the CEO and RSO will promptly share their decision(s), the underlying Risk Report, and internal feedback with both the Board and the LTBT.
units.paraphrase: After approval, the CEO and RSO will promptly share the decision, Risk Report, and internal feedback with the Board and LTBT.

units.excerpt: Modified process when marginal risk analysis is important to our case. In the event that marginal risk analysis (see previous section) plays a major role in a decision to move forward, explicit approval of the Risk Report by the Board and LTBT (rather than just the CEO and RSO) will be required.
units.paraphrase: If marginal risk analysis plays a major role in a decision to proceed, explicit Board and LTBT approval is required instead of only CEO and RSO approval.

units.excerpt: By "marginal risk analysis," we mean arguing that the risks imposed by our systems in particular are relatively lower when keeping in mind the risks unavoidably posed by other AI systems.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines marginal risk analysis as an argument comparing own-system risk to unavoidable risks posed by other AI systems.

units.excerpt: We will publish a public version of our Risk Report.
units.paraphrase: A public version of the Risk Report will be published.

units.excerpt: We will aim to minimize redactions to the public version of the report.
units.paraphrase: Redactions to the public version of the report will be minimized where possible.

units.excerpt: Reasons we may redact material include but are not limited to:
units.paraphrase: A non-exhaustive list of reasons for redaction follows.

units.context_stem: Reasons we may redact material include but are not limited to:
units.excerpt: Legal compliance: To comply with legal obligations on disclosing information, such as export control regulations, national security restrictions, or contractual obligations with third parties.
units.paraphrase: Redactions may be made to comply with legal obligations such as export controls, national security rules, or contracts.

units.context_stem: Reasons we may redact material include but are not limited to:
units.excerpt: Intellectual property protection: To protect proprietary information, including technical details of our models and training methodologies, trade secrets, or other confidential business information.
units.paraphrase: Redactions may protect proprietary information such as technical details, training methods, and trade secrets.

units.context_stem: Reasons we may redact material include but are not limited to:
units.excerpt: Public safety considerations: To protect public safety by not disclosing information that could be exploited to cause harm.
units.paraphrase: Redactions may protect public safety by withholding information that could be misused to cause harm.

units.context_stem: Reasons we may redact material include but are not limited to:
units.excerpt: Privacy: To protect the personal privacy of individuals.
units.paraphrase: Redactions may protect individuals' personal privacy.

units.excerpt: We will work toward a practice of seeking comprehensive, public external review on our Risk Reports.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic intends to work toward comprehensive, public external review of Risk Reports.

units.excerpt: This means working with one or more third-party organizations that will receive private versions of our Risk Reports (unredacted or with minimal redactions, as discussed below) and publish comprehensive commentary on them.
units.paraphrase: Third-party organizations will receive largely unredacted Risk Reports and publish comprehensive commentary.

units.excerpt: Commentary will address topics including the quality of our reasoning, the validity of our risk assessments, the overall level of risk, and whether the redactions we've made for the public version are reasonable and appropriate.
units.paraphrase: External commentary will cover reasoning quality, validity of assessments, overall risk level, and reasonableness of redactions.

units.excerpt: Our intent is for external reviewers' judgments to carry significant weight in the eyes of the public as well as our employees.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers' judgments are intended to carry significant weight with both the public and employees.

units.excerpt: But there are no well-established organizations or procedures for this sort of practice, and we are approaching it as an experiment.
units.paraphrase: Because no well-established organizations or procedures exist for this practice, it is being treated as an experiment.

units.excerpt: At a minimum, we will complete a full external review process (described below) with at least one external reviewer anytime a Risk Report covers highly capable models and is significantly redacted, defined as follows:
units.paraphrase: A full external review with at least one reviewer will be completed whenever a Risk Report covers highly capable models and is significantly redacted, as defined below.

units.excerpt: A model is "highly capable" if we conclude that it crosses the threshold for automated AI R&D described in Section 1.
units.paraphrase: A model is considered highly capable if it crosses the automated AI R&D threshold defined in Section 1.

units.excerpt: "Significantly redacted" means that the redactions omit information a reasonable external safety researcher would consider important in evaluating the overall level of risk, such that a reader of only the public version could not meaningfully assess whether they agree with our conclusions.
units.paraphrase: Significantly redacted means the omissions would prevent a reasonable external safety researcher from meaningfully assessing the risk conclusions from the public version alone.

units.excerpt: A report shall be deemed significantly redacted if, in the judgment of the RSO, CEO, Board, or LTBT, it meets this description.
units.paraphrase: The RSO, CEO, Board, or LTBT determine whether a report meets the significantly redacted definition.

units.excerpt: Note that unredacted reports will be shared with a large number of employees, who will be in a position to raise concerns if they believe the public version meets this description.
units.paraphrase: Unredacted reports are shared broadly with employees, who can raise concerns about the public version's redaction level.

units.excerpt: In consultation with the Board and LTBT, we will select external reviewers that:
units.paraphrase: External reviewers will be selected in consultation with the Board and LTBT, per the criteria below.

units.context_stem: we will select external reviewers that:
units.excerpt: Have significant experience and expertise regarding evaluations for dangerous AI capabilities and propensities.
units.paraphrase: Reviewers must have significant expertise in evaluating dangerous AI capabilities and propensities.

units.excerpt: It's particularly important that they be knowledgeable about potential ways such evaluations might be misleading (for example, alignment faking).
units.paraphrase: Reviewers should be knowledgeable about ways evaluations could be misleading, such as alignment faking.

units.context_stem: we will select external reviewers that:
units.excerpt: Have reputational and other incentives making them likely to be candid about their assessment of risks, rather than focused on writing comments that Anthropic will approve of.
units.paraphrase: Reviewers should have incentives favoring candor over pleasing Anthropic.

units.excerpt: For example, external review parties should not be teams whose revenue, reputation and success depend entirely on Anthropic and similar companies continuing to work with them.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers should not be entirely economically dependent on Anthropic and similar companies.

units.context_stem: we will select external reviewers that:
units.excerpt: Do not have conflicts of interest with respect to Anthropic.
units.paraphrase: Reviewers must not have conflicts of interest regarding Anthropic.

units.context_stem: Do not have conflicts of interest with respect to Anthropic.
units.excerpt: At a minimum, a reviewing organization itself may not have a financial interest in Anthropic; and the individuals involved in conducting the review, as well as anyone above them in the reporting chain within their organization, may not have a financial interest in Anthropic or close personal relationships with anyone at Anthropic (i.e., family relationships, romantic relationships, or shared living arrangements).
units.paraphrase: Neither the reviewing organization nor the individuals conducting the review (nor their superiors) may hold a financial interest in Anthropic or close personal relationships with Anthropic staff.

units.excerpt: The external review process will involve sharing the Risk Report with one or more external reviewers within one week of submitting the same report to our Board and LTBT.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers will receive the Risk Report within one week of its submission to the Board and LTBT.

units.excerpt: We will ask the external reviewers to provide public commentary on our report within 30 days of receipt.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers will be asked to publish commentary within 30 days of receiving the report.

units.excerpt: We will try to work toward a process that involves the full external review being completed prior to Board/LTBT review (and may require this later).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will attempt to complete full external review before Board/LTBT review, and may later make this mandatory.

units.excerpt: For purposes of external review, the only redactions to the Risk Report will be those necessary to comply with legal prohibitions or to maintain our legal rights.
units.paraphrase: Redactions for external review purposes are limited to those required for legal compliance or preserving legal rights.

units.excerpt: We expect that we will also invest some time in answering follow-up questions from parties doing external review.
units.paraphrase: Time is expected to be invested in answering follow-up questions from external reviewers.

units.excerpt: The external review will address:
units.paraphrase: The external review will cover the topics listed below.

units.excerpt: Adequacy of information: Whether the Risk Report contains sufficient information to assess the identified risks;
units.paraphrase: The review will assess whether the Risk Report contains sufficient information to evaluate identified risks.

units.excerpt: Analytical rigor: The strength of the Risk Report's reasoning and analysis;
units.paraphrase: The review will assess the strength of the report's reasoning and analysis.

units.excerpt: Areas of disagreement: Whether the external reviewer disagrees with any of the Risk Report's key claims and, if so, the reasons for any such disagreements; and
units.paraphrase: The review will note any disagreements with key claims and the reasons behind them.

units.excerpt: Risk reduction recommendations: Recommendations for further reducing identified risks.
units.paraphrase: The review will include recommendations for further reducing identified risks.

units.excerpt: The external reviewer will also evaluate our redaction decisions while avoiding disclosure of the redacted content itself.
units.paraphrase: The reviewer will also assess redaction decisions without disclosing the redacted material.

units.excerpt: In particular, the review will cover:
units.paraphrase: The review specifically covers the following redaction-related topics.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Redaction scope: The general nature and scope of redactions;
units.paraphrase: The review will describe the general nature and scope of redactions.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Redaction justification: Whether the external reviewer generally agrees or disagrees with the publicly stated reasons for the redactions and, if relevant, the reasons for any disagreements;
units.paraphrase: The review will state whether the reviewer agrees with the publicly stated redaction justifications and why, if disagreeing.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Balancing test: Whether the redactions strike a reasonable balance between Anthropic's legitimate interests and society's interest in transparency; and
units.paraphrase: The review will assess whether redactions reasonably balance Anthropic's interests against society's interest in transparency.

units.context_stem: In particular, the review will cover:
units.excerpt: Materiality: Whether any of the redactions in the public report are material to any of the external reviewer's substantive disagreements with the report's claims.
units.paraphrase: The review will assess whether redactions materially affect the reviewer's substantive disagreements with the report.

units.excerpt: Public comments. We will ask the external reviewer to memorialize its findings on the topics above in a written report that is made public.
units.paraphrase: External reviewers will be asked to produce a public written report memorializing their findings.

units.excerpt: External reviewers will be bound by obligations not to disclose confidential information (e.g., confidential intellectual property, matters of national security, or proprietary details such as model architecture, cost, or size), but beyond that will not be restricted in what they can publish, including concerns about the Risk Report or Anthropic's conduct in connection with the external review.
units.paraphrase: Reviewers must keep confidential information private but otherwise face no restriction on publishing concerns, including about Anthropic's conduct.

units.excerpt: For example, we may redact information if sharing it would endanger our legal right to treat it as confidential. This would be an uncommon situation.
units.paraphrase: The footnote gives an example: redacting information to preserve a legal right to confidentiality, noted as uncommon.

units.excerpt: It does not mean we would redact information merely because it is sensitive or to reduce the risk of a leak.
units.paraphrase: Sensitivity alone or leak-risk reduction alone is not sufficient justification for redaction under this footnote.

units.excerpt: We commit to the following governance measures to promote internal and external accountability.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to governance measures for internal and external accountability.

units.excerpt: Responsible Scaling Officer: We will maintain the position of RSO, a designated member of staff who is responsible for the implementation of this policy.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain an RSO position responsible for implementing the policy.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: (1) as needed, proposing updates to this policy; (2) approving relevant model development or deployment decisions based on our risk assessments; (3) reviewing major contracts (e.g., deployment partnerships) for consistency with this policy;
units.paraphrase: The RSO's duties include proposing policy updates, approving development/deployment decisions, and reviewing major contracts for policy consistency.

units.context_stem: The RSO's duties will include (but are not limited to):
units.excerpt: (4) overseeing the implementation of this policy, including the allocation of sufficient resources; (5) receiving and addressing reports of potential instances of noncompliance; and (6) making judgment calls on policy interpretation and application.
